title: cpu-side-bottlenecks-tokenization-threadpools-python-notes
content:
Summary:

This note captures recent CPU-side profiling and microbenchmarks focused on two recurring sources of latency and cost on the serving host: tokenization (BPE/wordpiece) and Python-side request handling (JSON parsing, uvicorn/ASGI overhead, thread-pool/GIL impacts). We did end-to-end profiling on the hosted inference stack (uvicorn + FastAPI -> request parsing -> tokenizer -> model runtime shim) to identify hotspots, quantify their impact across request shapes, and validate mitigations.

Background / motivation:
- Several customer reports and SLO miss incidents show disproportionate CPU use for short text generations (<= 32 tokens output).
- Profiling showed per-request CPU dominated by pre-model work (tokenization + request shims) for short sequences. For long sequences model decode dominates as expected.
- Goal: reduce median p50 latency and per-token CPU cost for short/interactive requests by addressing CPU-side bottlenecks.

Test environment and workload:
- Binary: serving-runtime commit 2b7f9d (baseline).
- Config: uvicorn + gunicorn (async workers), endpoint: /v1/generate, 16 worker processes in benchmark cluster, host r5.4xlarge equivalent CPU profile used for microbench.
- Workloads: three synthetic profiles: short-chat (req_len=8, prompt_len~16, response_max_tokens=16), medium (prompt 64, max_out 64), long (prompt 512, max_out 256).
- Batch settings: request-level batching disabled for baseline; separate microbench for batch size 8 and 32.
- Tooling: py-spy (flame), Linux perf, eBPF off-cpu, and simple time-based instrumentation around tokenizer and JSON handling.

Key profiling findings (p50/p95 contributions):
- Short-chat profile: tokenization (tokenizer.encode) 42% of CPU time on average, json.loads/json.dumps 19%, uvicorn.request handling + starlette routing ~12%, asyncio/await scheduling ~8%, other Python overhead (logging, metrics) ~6%, remaining time in model shim and small calls.
- Medium profile: tokenization ~28%, model shim + library calls increases, json parsing ~12%, scheduling ~10%.
- Long profile: model decode dominates (>70%), tokenization <10%.
- Thread pool observations: when using ThreadPoolExecutor for tokenization + small blocking tasks, the global interpreter lock (GIL) creates visible contention when we spawn many concurrent requests per process (py-spy shows many threads blocked on GIL and time spent in interpreter switching).
- Observed heavy memory churn during tokenization: temporary Python object allocations inside tokenizer wrapper (~15% of allocation profile).

Microbenchmarks and numbers (baseline):
- Single-request baseline (short-chat): p50 latency 78ms, p95 220ms. CPU time breakdown per-request: 63ms tokenization, 28ms json+request-shim, 12ms other, 18ms model shim (cold KV cache assumptions).
- Batch=8: tokenization cost amortizes slightly but serialization overhead increases; p50 110ms.
- Using ProcessPoolExecutor to isolate tokenization reduced p50 to 55ms (but increased memory and process overhead).

Root causes and analysis:
1) Tokenizer implementation in Python wrapper: we call a tokenizer (fastBPE) exposed via Python binding that still creates many temporary Python lists/strings per call. The hot path is Python-level splitting + calls into extension which serializes back into Python objects. The round-trip overhead dominates when actual model decode is cheap (short outputs).
2) JSON parsing/serialization using the stdlib json module is surprisingly expensive for our payload sizes and structure (lots of small keys).
3) ThreadPoolExecutor + GIL interaction: when using thread pools, CPU-bound tokenizer operations still contend on GIL because the extension doesn't release it fully or Python-level work remains. Worker count tuning is brittle: too many threads -> context switching and GIL stalls, too few -> queueing latency.
4) Async stack overhead: Starlette/uvicorn path allocates request and response objects and runs many small coroutine hops which add measurable latency in the p95. uvloop reduces overhead but not tokenization cost.

Mitigations evaluated (with data):
- Use orjson for parsing: replacing json.loads/dumps -> orjson yields ~2.5-3x speedup on parsing microbench; end-to-end p50 reduced by ~8-10ms for short-chat.
- Use fast Rust tokenizer binding (rust-tokenizers / tokenizers from HuggingFace): replacing current tokenizer API with tokenizers (C/Rust compiled) that returns bytes/ids without per-token Python allocations reduced tokenization CPU by ~55% in microbench. End-to-end p50 reduced from 78ms -> 44ms (short-chat).
- Offload tokenization to a dedicated process pool (ProcessPoolExecutor): eliminated GIL contention and reduced per-request latency but increased memory footprint (one process per CPU-bound worker). p50 ~55ms. Useful tradeoff for mid-term.
- Pre-tokenize client-side / edge caching: for trusted partners we can accept tokenized payloads; eliminates tokenization cost entirely. Small but effective for some partners.
- Introduce a C-extension wrapper that returns raw int arrays via PyCapsule (prototype): ~60% reduction vs baseline but higher engineering cost.
- Uvloop + pinned worker processes and tuned worker counts: improved scheduling overhead ~6ms p50.

Recommended immediate actions (0-2 weeks):
- Replace stdlib json with orjson in request parsing path (PR created, GH#482). Owner: Jordan Kim. Expected p50 improvement: ~10% for short requests.
- Add a feature flag to accept pre-tokenized input for trusted clients and internal benchmarks. Owner: Priya Kapoor.
- Prototype using HuggingFace tokenizers binding in a shadow mode (dual-run) to validate parity. Owner: Avery Chen. Deadline: 2026-03-05.

Medium-term (2-8 weeks):
- Migrate main tokenization path to Rust-backed tokenizers (or C-extension) to remove Python allocation overhead. Implement a thin C/Rust wrapper that returns contiguous int32 arrays to avoid per-token Python objects. Owner: Eng-Serving-Runtime + Applied-ML. Ticket: SRV-712.
- Evaluate ProcessPoolExecutor deployment patterns vs a dedicated tokenization service (gRPC/HTTP) that other processes call. Compare memory vs IPC costs. Owner: Ethan Morales.

Long-term (Q2+):
- Consider co-locating tokenization onto model-serving process using a shared native library (if memory and safety allow) to avoid IPC costs altogether.
- Add sampling flamegraphs & eBPF off-cpu tracing to prod by default for short requests (on-by-default low-overhead sampling).

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Memory vs latency: ProcessPool gives latency wins but increases memory and deployment complexity. Dedicated service introduces network hop but allows language-agnostic tokenizers and better scaling.
- Compatibility & safety for pre-tokenized inputs (replay attacks, mismatched tokenizers). Need signature/versioning scheme.
- How much engineering cost to accept for a C-extension vs adopting tokenizers from HF? Ownership and maintenance long-term.

Experiment notes / commands used:
- py-spy: py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid <pid> --native --duration 30 --subprocesses
- perf: perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30; perf script | flamegraph.pl > perf.svg
- JSON microbench: python -m timeit -s 'import json, payload' 'json.loads(payload)'
- orjson bench: python -m timeit -s 'import orjson, payload' 'orjson.loads(payload)'
- Tokenizer microbench: run tokenizers binding bench with 10k samples and measure allocations via tracemalloc and py-spy.

Action items (owner + ETA):
- Jordan Kim: PR to switch json->orjson + test harness (ETA: 2026-02-28).
- Priya Kapoor: feature flag for pre-tokenized input + edge docs (ETA: 2026-03-04).
- Avery Chen: run parity & perf tests for HF tokenizers in shadow mode (ETA: 2026-03-05).
- Ethan Morales: evaluate deployment patterns (ProcessPool vs dedicated service) and cost model (ETA: 2026-03-18).

Appendix: quick heuristics for teams
- If p50 short-request latency is >60ms and tokenization >30% of CPU: prioritize tokenizer migration or pre-tokenize clients.
- If GIL contention observed in py-spy: move CPU-heavy parts to process-based isolation rather than thread pools.
- Use orjson and uvloop as low-effort wins before large refactors.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add flamegraph images and attach to Confluence page once we sanitize customer payloads.
- Coordinate with security on accepting pre-tokenized payloads (malformed token ids).
- Run experiments on dedicated inference hardware profile (gpu-hosted vs cpu-hosted) to ensure consistent improvements.

End of note.
